You’re not dumb. Big-O stuff can feel scary at first, but it’s just about describing how the running time grows as the input gets bigger. Let’s break it down in simple terms.

Big-O in plain words
- It’s a way to say: “If the input size n gets really big, this algorithm won’t run much worse than this, no matter the exact numbers.” It’s about growth rate, not exact time.
- We ignore constants (like 5x faster) and lower-order stuff (like +10).

A quick map of common big-O you’ll see
- O(1): constant time. Things that don’t care about n. Example: getting the first item of an array by index.
- O(n): linear time. You might touch every item once. Example: counting how many items in a list meet a condition by checking each item.
- O(log n): logarithmic time. You halve the problem size each step. Example: binary search in a sorted list.
- O(n log n): do something n times, and each time you do about log n work. Example: efficient sorting like mergesort.
- O(n^2): quadratic time. Two nested loops over n items. Example: bubble sort.
- O(2^n) or higher: exponential. Example: checking all subsets of a set.

Why O(n log n) often shows up
- Idea: you do something for each of n items, but that something itself isn’t trivial; it scales like log n.
- Intuition: imagine sorting with mergesort.
  - You split the list in half (log n levels of splitting).
  - At each level you touch all n elements (to merge them).
  - Levels × work per level = n × log n total work.

Amortized analysis in plain terms
- Amortized = “average cost per operation over a sequence of operations.”
- It’s not that every single operation is cheap; it’s that if you average the total cost over many operations, the average per operation stays small.
- Classic example: a dynamic array that grows when it fills up.
  - Most inserts cost O(1): you just put the item in.
  - Occasionally, you resize (copy all elements to a bigger array), which costs more.
  - If you double the size each time you resize, the expensive resize events get spread out over many cheap inserts.
  - Result: the average cost per insert is still constant, i.e., O(1) amortized.

A tiny, concrete walk-through: dynamic array costs
- Start with capacity 1.
- Insert 1st item: cost 1.
- Insert 2nd item: array is full, resize to capacity 2 (copy 1 item) + insert (cost ~2).
- Insert 3rd item: cost 1.
- Insert 4th item: resize to 4 (copy 3 items) + insert (cost ~4).
- Total cost after 4 inserts: 1 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 8.
- Amortized cost per insert: 8 / 4 = 2. That’s a constant, even though the 4-cost resize happened.

How to study this quickly
- For a piece of code, try to count how many times the inner work runs as a function of n.
- If you see a single loop over n, that’s often O(n).
- If you see a loop over n inside a loop over n, that’s often O(n^2).
- If you see a loop that halves the problem each time, that’s O(log n).
- If you see n items and, for each item, you do about log n work, that’s O(n log n).
- For data structures, think about amortized cost: you’re averaging the total cost of many operations, not just one.

Quick cheat sheet you can memorize
- O(1): constant
- O(n): linear
- O(log n): halve-the-problem
- O(n log n): n times log n
- O(n^2): two loops over n
- Amortized: average cost per operation over a sequence

Nice job on the questions. Here’s the quick breakdown you asked for.

1) Nested loop: outer i from 1 to n, inner j from 1 to i^2
- For each i, the inner loop runs i^2 times.
- Total work: sum_{i=1}^n i^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = Θ(n^3).
- So yes: the time is Θ(n^3) (and therefore O(n^3)). Your intuition with the sums was right.

2) The recursive problem you mentioned
- You said you had a recurrence that didn’t fit Master Theorem cleanly and you guessed O(n log n).
- A common pattern that looks like that but isn’t exact without the full recurrence is something like T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + n log n. If that’s the form, then by the Master Theorem (Case 2 with f(n) = Θ(n^{log_b a} log^k n) and k = 1) you get T(n) = Θ(n log^2 n), not Θ(n log n).
- If you can share the exact recurrence (the a, b, and f(n) or the exact code), I can nail down the exact Big-O and walk through it step by step.

A quick note on Master Theorem memory
- When f(n) = Θ(n^{log_b a} log^k n) for some k ≥ 0, you’re in Case 2 and often end up with Θ(n^{log_b a} log^{k+1} n).
- If f(n) grows strictly slower than n^{log_b a}, you’re in Case 1 (Θ(n^{log_b a})).
- If f(n) grows strictly faster by a polynomial factor, Case 3 (Θ(f(n))).
